itens.explicacao: A gestão do tempo e a escolha da tarefa são parte da estratégia de exame.

licao.resumo: A primeira prova simulada reproduz o formato completo do C2 Proficiency com material novo: Reading and Use of English (sete partes), Writing (ensaio sobre arte pública e três tarefas à escolha), Listening e Speaking. Deve ser feita em condições de exame, com tempo cronometrado. Neste módulo praticam-se itens das Parts 1 a 5 e do Writing Part 1, aplicando as estratégias de cada tarefa: testar cada opção na expressão completa (Part 1), decidir a classe de palavra e verificar ambos os lados da lacuna (Parts 2 e 3), identificar o que a palavra-chave obriga (Part 4) e formar uma resposta antes de ler as opções (Part 5).
pontos: Part 1: colocações e expressões fixas — take their toll, on the verge of, set great store by, the litmus test, a bone of contention, a far cry from.
Part 2: uma palavra por lacuna; alvos frequentes são preposições, what-clefts e expressões fixas (Even so, as though).
Part 3: muitas vezes mais do que uma mudança (PRODUCE → counterproductive; BREAK → unbroken).
Part 4: duas metades por item — can't have meant | to offend.
Part 5: rejeitar opções que contradizem, exageram ou atribuem mal; a última pergunta pode ser global.
Writing Part 1: resumir e avaliar todos os pontos de ambos os textos e desenvolver a opinião própria.
licao.exemplo: Part 5 (p. 236, chave p. 337): na pergunta 36, a opção 'It has made him a fundamentally more patient person' é contrariada pelo texto ('not because I had become a patient person, which I have not'); a certa é 'It has influenced, if modestly, how he approaches problems elsewhere'.

itens.enunciado: Part 1: 'Pollution and hunting had ____ their toll, and by the 1970s the animal was on the verge of disappearing.'
itens.explicacao: Take its/their toll = causar danos (chave: 1 A).
porque: Certo: take their toll.
Make não forma a expressão.
Paid sugere pagar portagem, mas a expressão é take its toll.
Give não forma a expressão.

itens.enunciado: Part 1: 'Ecologists, however, set great ____ by their reappearance.'
itens.explicacao: Set great store by = dar grande importância a (chave: 5 C).
porque: Value não forma a expressão fixa com set.
Price não forma a expressão.
Certo: set great store by.
Weight forma outra colocação (attach weight to), não com set by.

itens.enunciado: Part 1: 'For fish farmers… the otter has become a bone of ____.'
itens.explicacao: A bone of contention = motivo de discórdia (chave: 7 C).
porque: Dispute não forma a expressão fixa.
Argument não forma a expressão fixa.
Certo: a bone of contention.
Conflict não forma a expressão fixa.

itens.enunciado: Part 2 (open cloze), 'The private page'. Write one word for each gap, separated by commas: 'Most were never intended (9) ____ publication… (10) ____ makes a diary valuable to historians is precisely its lack of polish.'
itens.modelo: for, What

itens.enunciado: Part 3 (word formation), 'The trouble with multitasking'. Write the words for: (18) 'a habit adopted to raise output turns out to be ____ (PRODUCE)'; (24) 'a period of ____ (BREAK) focus remains the most reliable route to quality'.

itens.explicacao: Dedução negativa no passado + mean to do (Unit 2).

itens.enunciado: Part 5. Read the extract from the personal essay 'The patience of old chairs' and answer the questions.
itens.excerto:
When I took up furniture restoration in my forties, I told friends it was a hobby, which was a way of lowering expectations, mainly my own. I had spent twenty years writing reports that were read once and filed. I wanted, I think, to make something that could be sat on.
The first lesson was humbling. My teacher, a retired cabinetmaker called Duarte, who had worked for the same workshop in Porto for thirty-eight years, handed me a chair with a broken stretcher and asked me what was wrong with it. I pointed to the break. He shook his head. The break, he explained, was the symptom; the problem was that someone, years before, had glued a loose joint instead of remaking it, and the strain had travelled along the frame until the weakest piece gave way. 'Most damage,' he said, 'is old repair.'

perguntas.enunciado: In the first paragraph, the writer suggests that he took up restoration partly because
opcoes: he wanted his work to have a more tangible result.
his friends had encouraged him to find a hobby.
he was dissatisfied with the quality of his reports.
he hoped to change his profession.
perguntas.explicacao: 'to make something that could be sat on' (chave: 31 A).
porque: Certo: queria fazer algo que se pudesse usar.
Ele próprio chamou-lhe hobby para baixar expectativas; os amigos não o incentivaram.
Critica o destino dos relatórios (lidos uma vez), não a sua qualidade.
Não diz que queria mudar de profissão.

perguntas.enunciado: What does Duarte's remark 'Most damage is old repair' refer to?
opcoes: the tendency of beginners to misdiagnose problems
the fragility of chairs made by inexperienced craftsmen
the way old furniture gradually weakens with use
harm caused by earlier attempts to fix a problem superficially
perguntas.explicacao: 'someone… had glued a loose joint instead of remaking it' (chave: 32 D).
porque: Duarte fala de reparações antigas, não de diagnósticos de principiantes.
Não fala de cadeiras mal feitas, mas de reparações mal feitas.
Não é o uso que enfraquece, é a reparação antiga.
Certo: colaram uma junta em vez de a refazer.

itens.explicacao: Questões 31–32 da prova simulada 1.

itens.enunciado: Part 5 (continued). Read another part of 'The patience of old chairs' and answer the questions.
itens.excerto:
Duarte was scathing about what he called 'dentist's work', the kind of refinishing that strips away a century of patina and leaves a piece looking like a reproduction of itself. A chair, in his view, should be allowed to admit its history. Not all his customers agreed. Some wanted their grandmother's sideboard to look as it had in a shop window in 1950, and he would occasionally turn the work down rather than do it.
There is a temptation, when writing about manual work, to sentimentalise it, and I am aware of having done so already. It is not all quiet satisfaction. Much of it is tedious, some of it is physically uncomfortable, and a good deal of it goes wrong. I have ruined more veneer than I care to admit. But the failures are instructive in a way that failures at a desk seldom are, because their causes are visible.

perguntas.enunciado: Duarte objected to 'dentist's work' because it
opcoes: was too expensive for most customers.
removed the evidence of a piece's age.
left visible marks of the repair.
required skills that few restorers possess.
perguntas.explicacao: 'strips away a century of patina' (chave: 34 B).
porque: Não se fala do custo para os clientes.
Certo: retira a pátina de um século.
Ele critica o contrário: a peça fica a parecer uma reprodução nova.
Não se fala de competências raras.

perguntas.enunciado: In the fifth paragraph, the writer
opcoes: argues that manual failures are more costly than intellectual ones.
regrets the time he has wasted on unsuccessful repairs.
claims that failure is less common in the workshop than at a desk.
admits that his account of manual work may have been idealised.
perguntas.explicacao: 'There is a temptation… to sentimentalise it, and I am aware of having done so' (chave: 35 D).
porque: Não diz que falhas manuais custam mais.
Admite falhas, mas não lamenta o tempo perdido.
Diz que as falhas são instrutivas, não menos frequentes.
Certo: admite ter idealizado o trabalho manual.

perguntas.enunciado: According to the writer, why are failures in the workshop more instructive than failures at a desk?
perguntas.modelo: Because their causes are visible: a joint that will not close tells you exactly what you did wrong.
perguntas.explicacao: A resposta está na última frase do excerto ('because their causes are visible').

itens.explicacao: Questões 34–35 da prova simulada 1 e uma pergunta aberta.

itens.enunciado: Writing Part 1. Text 1 (Art in public places): public art reaches people who never visit galleries, gives places an identity, the arguments it provokes bring residents into a conversation about their town, its cost is modest compared with a road junction, and a town without it chooses to be anonymous. Text 2 (Whose art?): too much public art is chosen by experts and imposed on residents who were never asked, who resent it because the money could have paid for services; it is valuable only when the community helps to choose or make it. Write an essay of 240–280 words summarising and evaluating the key points of both texts and developing your own view.
itens.modelo: Public art divides opinion more sharply than most items in a council budget, and the two texts take opposite views of why that matters. The first writer defends works of art in streets and squares. Such works are seen by people who would not normally visit a gallery; they give character to places that would otherwise have none; and the disputes they cause draw local people into a debate about the future of their town. Their price is small beside that of ordinary roadworks. The argument about reaching a wider audience is persuasive, and so is the idea that controversy can be productive. The final claim, however, that a town without such works has opted for anonymity, is overstated: character can come from architecture, markets or landscape as much as from sculpture. The second writer does not reject public art but questions the way it is selected. When experts choose a piece and residents are simply presented with it, resentment follows naturally, particularly if the funds could have paid for basic services. Art of this kind justifies itself only when the community helps to choose or create it. This is a fair criticism of a common practice, although it risks assuming that local preferences will always be wiser than expert judgement. In my view, the two positions can be reconciled. Public art deserves funding precisely because everyone encounters it, but for the same reason everyone should have a say in it.

criterios.ideia: Pontos do Texto 1 (público alargado, identidade, debate, custo modesto, anonimato)
Pontos do Texto 2 (imposta por peritos, dinheiro desviado de serviços, envolvimento da comunidade)

itens.explicacao: O ensaio-modelo (p. 338) tem banda 5 em todas as subescalas: todos os pontos resumidos e avaliados, opinião desenvolvida a partir dos dois textos.

licao.resumo: A segunda prova simulada segue o mesmo formato completo do C2 Proficiency. O Reading and Use of English trata pedidos de desculpa de empresas (Part 1), cidades caminháveis (Part 2), legendas de museus (Part 3) e um livro de memórias sobre aprender português aos quarenta e um anos (Part 5); o Writing Part 1 compara competição e cooperação na escola. Neste módulo praticam-se itens destas partes, com as mesmas estratégias: colocações e expressões fixas, classe de palavra e mudanças múltiplas, as duas metades da Part 4 e a localização do passo relevante antes de ler as opções.
pontos: Part 1: make or break, hedged with conditions, see through, pay lip service to, own up to, make excuses, set out, from the heart.
Part 2: Unlike…, in their own right, with cars in mind, even, more than, none of these, one corner at a time.
Part 3: KNOW → unknown; PENETRATE → impenetrable; TRIVIAL → trivialising; USE → useless; SCHOLAR → scholarly.
Part 4: If only I had accepted…; No sooner had she left than…; came as a surprise to…; may have been destroyed.
Part 5: as respostas certas parafraseiam o texto; distratores repetem palavras mudando a relação.
Writing Part 1: um bom ensaio nota que as posições estão mais próximas do que parecem e combina-as com uma razão.
licao.exemplo: Part 5, pergunta 33 (p. 250, chave p. 341): Dona Ermelinda ajudou porque 'she did not slow down or simplify… she did not seem to mind' — expôs o narrador ao discurso natural sem o pressionar; a opção 'she adapted her language to his level' contradiz o texto.

itens.explicacao: See through = perceber a falta de sinceridade (chave: 3 D).
porque: Look through é folhear, não perceber falsidade.
Notice through não existe.
Spot through não existe.
Certo: see through = perceber a falta de sinceridade.

itens.enunciado: Part 1: 'An apology that comes too late, or that is ____ with conditions, often does more harm than good.'
itens.explicacao: Hedged with conditions = rodeado de condições (chave: 2 B).
porque: Fenced with conditions não é a colocação.
Certo: hedged with conditions.
Walled não colocaliza com conditions.
Bordered não colocaliza com conditions.

itens.enunciado: Part 1: 'it owns ____ to the mistake, it explains what went wrong without making excuses'
itens.explicacao: Own up to = admitir (chave: 5 B).
porque: Own in não existe.
Certo: own up to = admitir.
Own out não existe.
Own off não existe.

itens.enunciado: Part 2 (open cloze), 'In praise of walking cities'. Write one word for each gap, separated by commas: '(9) ____ the driver, who sees streets as obstacles…, the walker experiences them as places in (10) ____ own right.'
itens.modelo: Unlike, their
itens.explicacao: Unlike introduz o contraste; in their own right é expressão fixa.

itens.enunciado: Part 3 (word formation), 'Rethinking the museum label'. Write the words for: (18) 'many visitors found them ____ (PENETRATE)'; (21) 'risk ____ (TRIVIAL) the objects they describe'.
itens.modelo: (18) impenetrable (21) trivialising
itens.explicacao: (18) prefixo im- + sufixo -able; (21) risk + -ing com verbo derivado em -ise.

itens.enunciado: Part 4. 'I regret not accepting the job in Lisbon.' ONLY → If ________ the job in Lisbon.
itens.modelo: If only I had accepted the job in Lisbon.
itens.explicacao: If only + past perfect para arrependimento sobre o passado (Unit 3).

itens.enunciado: Part 4. 'Everyone was surprised that he resigned.' CAME → His resignation ________ everyone.
itens.modelo: His resignation came as a surprise to everyone.
itens.explicacao: Expressão fixa: come as a surprise to somebody.

itens.modelo: I had no idea how much work the project involved.
itens.explicacao: Have no idea + pergunta indireta.

itens.enunciado: Part 5. Read the extract from the memoir 'Late Portuguese' and answer the questions.
itens.excerto:
The first months were spent in a state I came to think of as polite deafness. I could buy bread and ask for the bill, but conversation passed over me like weather. Portuguese, as spoken in Lisbon, swallows its vowels; whole syllables that I had learnt from the book simply failed to appear. I would rehearse a question on the way to the café, ask it perfectly, and then understand nothing of the answer, which was usually friendly and always fast. At work, meetings were held in English for my benefit, which was kind and entirely counterproductive.
What changed things was not a course, though I took several, but a neighbour. Dona Ermelinda was eighty, lived on the floor below, and had decided, without consulting me, that I was too thin. She began leaving soup at my door, and when I went down to return the pots, she talked. She talked about her late husband, the price of fish, the scandal of the new tram timetable, and she did not slow down or simplify anything for my benefit. I understood perhaps a tenth of it. But she did not seem to mind, and after a while I stopped minding too.

perguntas.enunciado: What does the writer mean by 'polite deafness'?
opcoes: He pretended not to understand in order to avoid conversation.
He was too shy to ask people to repeat themselves.
He could manage simple exchanges but could not follow real conversation.
He found local people unwilling to talk to him.
perguntas.explicacao: 'I could buy bread… but conversation passed over me' (chave: 32 C).
porque: Ele não fingia; não conseguia acompanhar.
O texto não fala de timidez em pedir para repetir.
Certo: trocas simples sim, conversa real não.
As pessoas falavam com ele, amigavelmente.

perguntas.enunciado: Dona Ermelinda's conversations were helpful because
opcoes: she adapted her language to his level.
she taught him the vocabulary he needed in daily life.
she exposed him to natural speech, without pressure.
perguntas.explicacao: 'she did not slow down or simplify… she did not seem to mind' (chave: 33 D).
porque: Ela não abrandava nem simplificava.
O texto não diz que ela o corrigia.
Falava de tudo, sem ensinar vocabulário.
Certo: fala natural sem pressão.

perguntas.enunciado: Why does the writer describe the meetings held in English as 'kind and entirely counterproductive'?
perguntas.modelo: They were kind because colleagues wanted to help him, but counterproductive because they deprived him of the exposure to Portuguese he needed in order to learn.
perguntas.explicacao: A inferência deve poder ligar-se ao texto: as reuniões em inglês tiravam-lhe contacto com a língua.

itens.explicacao: Questões 32–33 da prova simulada 2 e uma pergunta de inferência.

itens.enunciado: Part 5 (continued). Read another part of 'Late Portuguese' and answer the questions.
itens.excerto:
I have read since that adults learn languages less efficiently than children, and I do not doubt it. But the comparison misses something. A child learns without knowing what it is losing; an adult learns in full awareness of being, for a long time, a diminished version of himself. In English I am, I like to think, reasonably articulate. In Portuguese I was, for two years, a man who could not make a joke, could not disagree subtly, could not tell a story without the ending collapsing into gestures.
It was also, though I only saw this later, an education in attention. Because I could not rely on words, I learnt to watch faces, to notice tone, to wait. Dona Ermelinda's stories had a shape I could follow long before I could follow the sentences: a rising indignation, a pause, a punchline delivered with a flat hand on the table. I began to anticipate the pause.

perguntas.enunciado: In the fourth paragraph, the writer argues that adult learners
opcoes: learn more efficiently than research suggests.
are conscious of losing the identity their first language gives them.
should avoid comparing themselves with children.
need a strong sense of self-esteem in order to succeed.
perguntas.explicacao: 'in full awareness of being… a diminished version of himself' (chave: 34 B).
porque: Ele aceita que os adultos aprendem menos eficientemente.
Certo: consciência de ser uma versão diminuída de si.
Ele faz a comparação com crianças; não diz para a evitar.
Diz que não recomendaria a quem depende de ser compreendido, não que é preciso autoestima.

perguntas.enunciado: What does the writer say he gained from his difficulties?
opcoes: an ability to read meaning beyond words
a better understanding of Portuguese humour
a closer friendship with his colleagues
perguntas.explicacao: 'I learnt to watch faces, to notice tone' (chave: 35 A).
porque: Certo: aprendeu a ler rostos e tom.
Não fala de humor português em geral.
Diz que não conseguia contar histórias.
Não fala de amizade com colegas.

itens.explicacao: Questões 34–35 da prova simulada 2.

itens.enunciado: Writing Part 1. Text 1 (The case for competition): children compete anyway, school is a place to learn to win and lose with grace, comparison raises standards, the danger is competitions only a few can win. Text 2 (Learning together): public rankings tell most pupils they are not good enough and teach that effort is pointless; cooperation rewards all contributors and reflects adult teamwork; pupils should be measured against their own earlier performance. Write an essay of 240–280 words summarising and evaluating both texts and developing your own view.
itens.modelo: Few questions in education provoke as much feeling as the place of competition, and the two texts reach opposite conclusions from a shared concern for pupils. The first writer argues that rivalry is already part of children's lives and that school offers a safe setting in which to learn how to handle both success and failure. Being compared with classmates also makes pupils more careful with their work. The writer concedes, however, that contests which almost nobody can win do real harm. The point about learning to lose gracefully is convincing, and the concession is important, since it moves the argument from whether pupils should compete to how. The second writer focuses on what public rankings do to the majority. Such lists tell most children that they are failing and so discourage effort, whereas cooperation rewards all who contribute and reflects the teamwork of adult life. This is not a case for lower standards but for judging each pupil against his or her own earlier performance. This is persuasive, although the claim that adults mostly work in teams is a generalisation. The two positions are closer than they first appear. In my view, the most sensible approach combines them: competition in low-stakes settings, such as sport or quizzes, where losing teaches resilience, and assessment based on individual progress where a child's confidence is at stake.

itens.enunciado: Part 5. Read the extract from 'What the map leaves out' and answer the questions.
itens.excerto:
A map cannot show everything. Even the most detailed street plan leaves out far more than it includes: the smell of the bakery, the steepness that makes a street unbearable in August, the corner where everyone knows not to linger at night. The cartographer chooses, and every choice is a judgement about what matters. When I was learning, my teacher made us draw the same village three times, once for a walker, once for a tax inspector and once for a child, and then asked us which was the true one. The walker's map was all paths and gradients; the inspector's was all boundaries; the child's had the sweet shop at the centre and the church nowhere at all. The answer, of course, was that none of them was, or all of them were.
Digital maps have not removed these choices; they have hidden them. Because they can zoom endlessly, they give the impression of containing everything, of being not a description of the world but the world itself. The decisions are still made, but by algorithms and commercial agreements that nobody sees.

itens.enunciado: Part 5 (continued). Read the end of 'What the map leaves out' and answer the questions.
itens.excerto:
A paper map announced its maker. It had a title, a date, a scale and, often, a name in the corner. Some makers hid small inventions in their work, a street that did not exist or a hamlet that nobody lived in, so that copies could be detected. Even these traps were a kind of signature. You knew that someone had drawn it, and you could ask what that person had wanted you to see. The screen in your hand has no corner and no name. It presents itself as neutral, and that, I think, is the most persuasive argument a map has ever made.
None of this means that we should go back. I use digital maps every day, and I would not want to find my way around an unfamiliar city without one. I have followed one, on a bad day, into a dead end, and blamed myself rather than the map. But I wish they came with a small reminder, somewhere on the screen, that they too were drawn by someone, for someone, and that what they leave out may matter as much as what they show.

itens.enunciado: Writing Part 1. Text 1 (Famous examples): public figures shape young people's ambitions and can change attitudes faster than government campaigns, so fame brings obligations; those who complain chose the spotlight. Text 2 (Closer to home): celebrity success is narrow, due to talent or luck, and reaches us through managed images; young people learn more from adults they know; holding celebrities to moral standards distracts us from ordinary examples. Write an essay of 240–280 words summarising and evaluating both texts and developing your own view.
itens.modelo: Both texts accept that young people need examples to follow; they disagree about where to find them and what we may ask of them. The first writer argues that celebrities, willingly or not, influence what young people hope to become, and that a single gesture, such as a sportsman admitting to depression, can shift attitudes more quickly than official campaigns. Influence of this kind carries duties as well as advantages, and stars who resent the burden should recall that their visibility was their own choice. Their reach is hard to dispute. The claim that fame is always chosen is less convincing: many athletes and musicians become well known as teenagers, before they could understand what celebrity demands. The second writer shifts the focus from the famous to the familiar. Celebrity success is narrow, often owed to rare gifts or luck, and reaches the public in carefully controlled form; the adults in a young person's daily life are more instructive. Expecting moral perfection from stars blinds us to the worth of these everyday models. This is a persuasive corrective, although it may underestimate how much a distant figure can inspire someone whose surroundings offer few examples. In my view, both writers are partly right. Famous people do have unusual influence, but treating them as the main source of moral guidance is a mistake. Schools and communities would do better to make ordinary achievements visible.
